description: AstraForge is a student team competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge to build an innovative project using NASA data. We’re interested in AI, space exploration, astronaut safety, and interactive software. We’re looking for motivated developers, designers, researchers, and anyone excited about space and building something competitive.
summary: Astraxis is an SI-powered research dashboard that turns NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insight scientists can trust. We cleaned and unified 403 test records from two ISS investigations, FLEX (PSI-69, 274 droplet-combustion tests) and BASS-II (PSI-25, 129 solid-fuel tests), into one searchable, documented dataset. It also ranks all 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s PSI catalog for habitat fire safety, shows which tests come closest to planned Moon-base air (30% oxygen or more at about 10.2 psi), compares SAFFIRE spacecraft-material fires, predicts flame-out with a cross-validated model, and offers a Habitat Fire Lab that refuses to guess where NASA never tested, then lists what NASA should test next. Users can compare how oxygen, pressure, diluent gas and airflow relate to flame extinction, explore every test alongside NASA’s original record, and ask an AI research assistant questions in plain language. The assistant answers only from matching NASA records, cites every test it uses, separates observations from interpretation, and states the limits of the evidence. It never predicts Moon or Mars behaviour, because PSI contains no partial-gravity data. This matters because future spacecraft and habitats are planned with oxygen-enriched, low-pressure atmospheres, and fire-safety decisions need evidence that is traceable back to NASA’s measurements rather than guesses.
details:
What it does

Astraxis summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA PSI microgravity combustion investigations through eleven views:

  • Overview: what the two investigations studied, how many tests each contains, and the headline findings.
  • Habitat Fire Lab: pick any oxygen level and cabin pressure on a map coloured by our flame-out model, including NASA’s planned habitat atmospheres (26.5% oxygen at 10.2 psi and 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi). An animated droplet flame burns at the predicted rate. Where NASA never tested (below 10.17 psi or above 34% oxygen), the Lab refuses to predict and links to the evidence gaps.
  • Compare: interactive charts of outcome vs oxygen concentration, diluent gas (N2, CO2, He) and pressure, each with a table view and hover details.
  • Habitat conditions: which NASA tests come closest to planned Moon-base air (30% oxygen or more at about 0.7 atm). In the 17 nearest FLEX tests, none ended with the flame going out, compared with 25 of 26 at the same pressure with less than 20% oxygen.
  • Spacecraft materials: the 13 material samples NASA burned in the SAFFIRE experiments aboard Cygnus cargo ships, each compared with the same material burned in normal gravity. In SAFFIRE-II, 5 samples burned less in microgravity, 2 burned their full length in both, 1 burned in neither, and 1 could not be compared.
  • Investigations ranked: all 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s PSI catalog, scored on five habitat fire-safety criteria (habitat-level oxygen, low pressure, spacecraft materials, fire-safety use, flight data). Every mark is backed by a quote from NASA’s catalog entry.
  • Flame-out model: a logistic regression trained on all 261 FLEX tests with a known outcome gives the chance that a droplet flame goes out, from oxygen, pressure, fuel, diluent gas and droplet size. Checked with 5-fold cross-validation repeated 20 times, it is right 83% of the time (AUC 0.88), versus 69% for always guessing the most common outcome.
  • Evidence gaps: four conditions NASA has never tested, counted straight from the data. For example, none of the 24 tests at 10.2 psi or lower used 30% oxygen or more, and none of the 142 solid-material tests did either. These are the tests we recommend NASA run next.
  • Explorer: every one of the 403 tests, filterable, with a detail panel showing the cleaned values next to NASA’s original row and any data-quality flags.
  • Research Assistant: ask a question in plain English. Astraxis finds and ranks the matching tests, then an AI model writes a cited answer in three parts: what the NASA data shows, a hedged interpretation, and the limits of the evidence. For questions about which investigations matter most, the ranking list is inserted by the server straight from the data, so the AI cannot misstate it.
  • Sources: every NASA file used, the field dictionary, and a log of every cleaning decision.

What the data shows (FLEX, PSI-69)

Below 20% oxygen, 108 of 122 droplet tests ended in flame extinction (methanol 75 of 76, heptane 33 of 46). At 24% oxygen and above, 34 of 49 tests ended in droplet disruption instead. As oxygen falls, more of the droplet is left unburned when the flame goes out. BASS-II (PSI-25) records test conditions (oxygen, airflow, sample) but not outcomes in its data table, so we present it as a conditions map and say so.

How it works

  1. A Python pipeline reads NASA’s raw CSV and Excel files, handles their Windows-1252 encoding and “no value” markers, standardizes units and field names, and flags suspect values instead of silently deleting them. For example, one BASS-II test has an impossible final oxygen reading of 40.4%. Every change is written to a cleaning log.
  2. The cleaned data feeds a Next.js web app. Charts are built from the data directly, with colorblind-checked palettes.
  3. The Research Assistant retrieves before it writes. It parses the question (fuel, gas, oxygen range, investigation), ranks the matching tests, and spreads the evidence across oxygen levels so one band cannot dominate. Only those records go to the language model. The server then checks every test ID the model cites against the evidence it was given, and marks anything else as unverified.
  4. The investigation ranking scores every entry in NASA’s PSI catalog on five criteria, and each mark stores the exact catalog sentence that justifies it, so the AI never invents a ranking.
  5. The flame-out model is fit in Python with scikit-learn, checked with 5-fold cross-validation repeated 20 times and a calibration test by oxygen band, then exported to the web app so predictions run instantly in the browser.

Benefits

  • Researchers and fire-safety engineers get one consistent, documented view of investigations that were previously separate files with different formats.
  • Every number traces back to a NASA record, so findings can be checked.
  • The assistant is honest by design: it states uncertainty, flags unverified units, and refuses to extrapolate to partial gravity.

Goals

Help identify the conditions (oxygen, pressure, diluent) most relevant to spacecraft and future habitat atmospheres, and make PSI combustion data easier to use for modeling and fire-safety equipment research.

Tools and languages

TypeScript, Python (scikit-learn), Next.js (React), Tailwind CSS, Motion, Azure OpenAI (gpt-4.1-mini), hosted on Vercel, source on GitHub.
